leadership.principle: A true leader protects what is nearly broken rather than finishing it off. It costs nothing to snap a bruised reed; tenderness fans the dying flame back to life.
leadership.innerLife: The Servant handles the barely-surviving with exquisite care. A leader formed here develops restraint toward the fragile, refusing the ease of breaking what is already bruised. The inner work is gentleness strong enough to protect a flickering flame.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Handle the bruised and smoldering with extra care — the crushed confidence, the flickering motivation. Cup your hand around dying flames instead of snuffing them. Bring truth and justice, but without breaking the fragile in the process.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders break bruised reeds with careless words and never notice the cost, because finishing off the fragile is so easy. The blind spot is not seeing who is barely hanging on when you speak.
leadership.difficultConversations: With someone barely smoldering, the manner matters as much as the message. The same truth can either snap the reed or, delivered gently, help it heal.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify one bruised, barely-smoldering person around you. This week, handle them with deliberate gentleness, and fan the flame rather than risk snuffing it.
teamQuestions: Who comes to us bruised and barely smoldering?
Where might a careless word be snapping a fragile reed?
Are we protecting dying flames or snuffing them out?
Can we bring truth without breaking the fragile?

title: Beside still waters
moment:
The most famous shepherd psalm pictures the LORD doing something many leaders never do for their people: he makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside still waters, he restores my soul. Sheep will not lie down when they are anxious, hungry, or harassed; rest requires a shepherd who has first provided safety and provision. And then the shepherd actively leads them — to restoration, not just to the next pasture.

Driven leaders are skilled at leading people to work and poor at leading them to rest. They provide targets, pressure, the next hill to take — but never the still waters. Yet part of shepherding is restoring souls: building in the green pastures and quiet places where people are replenished rather than merely deployed. A flock run ragged cannot follow far. The shepherd who only drives, and never leads his people to rest, will eventually have nothing left to lead.
voiceQuote: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
scriptureText: He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
weight:
Driven leaders are good at leading people to work and poor at leading them to rest — always the next hill, never the still waters. But a flock run ragged cannot follow far.

Are you leading your people to rest and restoration, or only to the next demand?

notes.primary: Psalm 23:1–3 (he leads beside still waters and restores the soul); Matthew 11:28 (come to me and I will give you rest).

leadership.principle: A good shepherd leads people to rest, not just to work — to green pastures and still waters where souls are restored, not merely deployed.
leadership.innerLife: The shepherd of the psalm actively leads the flock to restoration. A leader formed here values rest and replenishment for his people, not only output. The inner work is resisting the drive that only ever points to the next hill.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Build in green pastures and still waters — margin, restoration, real rest — for the people you lead. Lead them to replenishment, not just to the next demand. Protect the flock from being run ragged, knowing the exhausted cannot follow far.
leadership.blindSpot: Driven leaders measure care by how much they ask and never lead anyone to rest. The blind spot is running the flock ragged and mistaking relentless demand for leadership.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a team is depleted, the needed permission is to lead them to rest. A shepherd who only drives will soon have nothing left to lead.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Notice where your people are run ragged. This week, lead them to one concrete place of rest or restoration, not just the next task.
teamQuestions: Are we leading people to rest, or only to the next demand?
Where is our flock being run ragged?
Do we build in still waters, or only more hills?
Is restoration part of how we lead, or an afterthought?

title: Let the children come
moment:
People were bringing little children to Jesus, and the disciples — busy, important, guarding the great teacher's time — rebuked them and shooed them away. Children had no status, nothing to offer, no claim on a rabbi's attention. Jesus was indignant. Let the little children come to me, he said; don't hinder them, for the Kingdom of God belongs to such as these. And he took them in his arms and blessed them.

The disciples' instinct is every busy leader's instinct: protect your time for the people who matter — those with influence or usefulness — and wave away the rest. Jesus reverses it. He makes time for exactly the ones the system deemed unimportant. A leader reveals his heart most clearly by how he treats those who can do nothing for him: the junior, the unconnected, the ones others are quietly shooing out of the room. To them, Jesus gave his arms and his blessing.
voiceQuote: Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, on receiving a child — Matthew 18:5 (WEB)
scriptureText: Allow the little children to come to me! Don't forbid them, for the Kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
weight:
Every busy leader's instinct is to protect his time for the people who matter and wave away the rest. Jesus made time for exactly the ones the system waved away.

Whom are you shooing out of the room as unimportant — and what would making time for them reveal about your heart?

notes.primary: Mark 10:13–16 (let the children come; the kingdom belongs to such); Matthew 18:5 (receiving a child receives Christ).

leadership.principle: A leader reveals his heart by how he treats those who can do nothing for him. The Christlike instinct makes time for the overlooked the system waves away.
leadership.innerLife: Jesus was indignant at gatekeeping that protected his time from the unimportant. A leader formed here resists guarding his attention only for the useful and influential. The inner work is a heart that values the ones who can offer nothing in return.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Make deliberate time for the junior, the unconnected, the overlooked. Refuse to let busyness turn into gatekeeping that shoos away the unimportant. Treat those who can do nothing for you as worth your arms and your blessing.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders protect their time for the influential and call it stewardship, while waving away the lowly. The blind spot is not seeing that how they treat the useless-to-them reveals their actual heart.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a culture quietly sidelines the low-status, the corrective is to bring them back into the room. Whom a leader makes time for teaches the whole team who matters.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify someone you tend to wave away as unimportant. This week, make real time for them, expecting nothing in return.
teamQuestions: Whom are we shooing out of the room as unimportant?
Does our calendar protect time only for the useful?
How do we treat those who can do nothing for us?
What does our gatekeeping reveal about our hearts?

title: Serve them, and they will follow
moment:
The old men who had served Solomon gave young King Rehoboam the wisest counsel of his reign: if you will be a servant to these people today, and serve them, and speak kind words to them, then they will be your servants forever. Serve them first, and they will follow you for life. Rehoboam rejected it, listened to his peers, threatened the people with heavier burdens instead — and split the kingdom in a single day.

The counsel exposes the order most leaders get backwards. They demand that people serve the vision before they have served the people; they ask for a loyalty they have not earned. The elders saw that service flows downhill first. A leader who genuinely, sacrificially serves his people — before asking anything of them — wins a devotion that no amount of demand can produce. Rehoboam wanted servants without being one, and was left with a fraction of a kingdom to rule.
voiceQuote: The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, on why he came — Matthew 20:28 (WEB)
scriptureText: If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever.
weight:
Leaders demand that people serve the vision before they have served the people, asking a loyalty they haven't earned. Rehoboam wanted servants without being one — and split a kingdom in a day.

Are you serving your people before asking them to serve your vision, or demanding a loyalty you haven't earned?

notes.primary: 1 Kings 12:1–17 (the elders counsel Rehoboam to serve the people; he refuses and loses the kingdom); Matthew 20:28 (Christ came to serve).

leadership.principle: Service flows downhill first. Serve your people before asking them to serve your vision, and you win a devotion no demand can produce.
leadership.innerLife: The elders knew loyalty is earned by serving, not commanded. A leader formed here serves his people first rather than demanding they serve his vision. The inner work is the humility to lead by serving, as Rehoboam would not.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Serve your people genuinely and sacrificially before asking anything of them. Speak good words and bear their burdens, and let followership grow from that. Refuse the Rehoboam path of demanding loyalty you have not earned.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders ask people to serve the vision while never serving the people, then resent the lack of devotion. The blind spot is demanding a loyalty that only service can earn.
leadership.difficultConversations: When loyalty is thin, the honest question is whether the leader has served the people first. Rehoboam’s ruin warns against answering low devotion with heavier demands.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify a place you are demanding service or loyalty. This week, reverse it — serve those people first, concretely, before asking anything.
teamQuestions: Are we serving our people before asking them to serve the vision?
Where are we demanding loyalty we haven’t earned?
Do we answer low devotion with heavier demands?
What would serving them first look like here?

title: My true child in the faith
moment:
Paul opens his letter to Timothy with a phrase that carries a whole relationship: to Timothy, my true child in the faith. Timothy was not merely a staff member or a project. He was a son Paul had begotten in the gospel, mentored over years, sent on hard missions, corrected, encouraged, and loved. Across two letters we watch an aging leader pour himself into a younger one with a father's investment.

This is mentoring at its deepest — not a program, but a paternity. Paul did not just teach Timothy skills; he gave him himself, took responsibility for his formation, and claimed him as a son. Much leadership development stays shallow because it is impersonal: a course, a curriculum, a hurried word. The kind that actually forms people is costly and relational — investing in specific individuals over the long haul, the way Paul invested in Timothy. Every leader should be raising up at least one true child in the faith.
voiceQuote: In Christ Jesus I became your father through the Good News.
scriptureText: to Timothy, my true child in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
weight:
Much leadership development is shallow because it is impersonal — a course, a curriculum, a hurried word. The kind that actually forms people is costly, relational, and long.

Whom are you investing in deeply enough to call, like Paul, a true child in the faith?

notes.primary: 1 Timothy 1:2 (Timothy, Paul’s true child in the faith); 1 Corinthians 4:15 (Paul became their father through the gospel).

leadership.principle: The deepest development is a paternity, not a program. Forming a leader means investing yourself in specific individuals over the long haul, the way Paul did Timothy.
leadership.innerLife: Paul claimed Timothy as a son, not a project, and gave him himself. A leader formed here takes personal, costly responsibility for raising up others. The inner work is loving people enough to invest in their formation over years.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Invest deeply and personally in a few you are raising up, not just broadly and impersonally in many. Give them yourself — correction, encouragement, real responsibility — over the long haul. Aim to have at least one true child in the faith.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders mistake courses and curricula for development and never invest personally in anyone. The blind spot is treating formation as a program when it is fundamentally relational.
leadership.difficultConversations: Mentoring includes the hard, fatherly words — correction and challenge given over years. It is the relationship, not a single talk, that forms a true child in the faith.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Name one person you could raise up as Paul raised Timothy. This week, take a concrete step to invest in them personally and for the long haul.
teamQuestions: Whom are we investing in deeply enough to call a true child in the faith?
Is our development personal, or just programs and courses?
Who is taking responsibility for forming the next generation?
Are we investing in a few over the long haul?

title: Spend and be spent
figure: Paul pours himself out for Corinth
moment:
The Corinthians had wounded Paul — questioned his authority, preferred flashier leaders, taken his labor for granted. And still he writes: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less? He will pour out his resources and his very self for people who do not fully appreciate it — and not grudgingly, but gladly.

Spend and be spent is the language of total expenditure: not giving merely from the surplus, but being used up, like a candle that gives light by consuming itself. And Paul's wry question about being loved less names the hardest part of shepherding — loving people who will not love you back in equal measure, pouring into those who take it for granted. The mark of a true shepherd is that he keeps spending himself anyway, gladly, because his giving is not a transaction. He is not buying their affection; he is loving their souls.
voiceQuote: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
scriptureText: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less?
weight:
Shepherding often means loving people who will not love you back in equal measure — pouring into those who take it for granted. Paul did it gladly anyway, because his giving was not a transaction.

Are you willing to spend and be spent for people who may never fully appreciate it — and to do it gladly?

notes.primary: 2 Corinthians 12:15 (gladly spend and be spent for your souls); John 10:11 (the good shepherd lays down his life).

leadership.principle: Shepherding pours itself out for people gladly, even when love is not returned in kind. The shepherd spends himself to love souls, not to buy affection.
leadership.innerLife: Paul kept spending himself for people who undervalued him, and did it gladly. A leader formed here gives without making it a transaction, free of the need to be repaid in love. The inner work is loving souls more than being appreciated.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Pour yourself out for your people without keeping score of the return. Expect to love some who will not love you back equally, and serve them gladly anyway. Spend yourself for souls, not for applause or reciprocity.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders quietly meter their giving to the appreciation they receive. The blind spot is making love a transaction, so care dries up where it is not repaid.
leadership.difficultConversations: When resentment builds at being undervalued, the freeing truth is that shepherding is not a transaction. Paul’s gladness despite being loved less reframes the giving.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify someone you serve who rarely appreciates it. This week, spend yourself for them gladly, without expecting anything back.
teamQuestions: Are we willing to spend and be spent for the unappreciative?
Where has our giving become a transaction?
Do we meter care to the return we get?
Can we love souls more than being appreciated?

title: Imitate me as I imitate Christ
figure: Paul offers his life as a model
moment:
Paul makes a claim that would be sheer arrogance if it were not so accountable: imitate me, as I imitate Christ. He knew people learn leadership and faith less from what they are told than from what they watch. So he offered his own life as a model — but a model anchored to a higher one. Follow me, he says, but only insofar as I am following Christ.

Two truths sit inside that sentence. First, you are being imitated whether you intend it or not; the people you lead are watching your life and quietly copying it. Second, your example is only safe to follow as far as you yourself are following Christ. The call to be imitated is also a call to be imitable — to live a life you would actually want reproduced in others. Leaders who say do as I say, not as I do have already failed, because the doing is the real teaching. The most powerful curriculum a leader has is the example of his own life.
voiceQuote: In all things show yourself an example of good works.
scriptureText: Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.
weight:
You are being imitated whether you intend it or not — those you lead are copying your life, not just your instructions. The only question is whether your example is safe to follow.

Is your life one you would actually want reproduced in the people you lead?

notes.primary: 1 Corinthians 11:1 (imitate me as I imitate Christ); Titus 2:7 (show yourself an example of good works).

leadership.principle: Leaders teach most by example. You are imitated whether you intend it or not, and your life is only safe to follow as far as you follow Christ.
leadership.innerLife: Paul could say imitate me only because he was following Christ. A leader formed here lives a life he would want reproduced, knowing he is always being watched. The inner work is becoming imitable, not just instructive.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Lead by the example of your own life, not just your words, and keep that example anchored to Christ. Recognize you are always being copied, and live accordingly. Make your conduct the curriculum you would want learned.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders rely on instruction and forget their life is the louder teacher. The blind spot is do as I say, not as I do — not seeing that the doing is what is actually reproduced.
leadership.difficultConversations: When words and example diverge, people follow the example. The honest reckoning is whether a leader’s life is one he would want copied.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Examine one habit your team is likely copying from you. This week, bring it into line with what you would actually want reproduced in them.
teamQuestions: Is our life one we would want reproduced in our people?
Where does our example contradict our instructions?
Are we anchored closely enough to Christ to be imitated?
What are people copying from us that we never taught?

title: Comfort with the comfort you received
moment:
Paul calls God the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, and then names the purpose of comfort received: that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction with the comfort we ourselves received from God. The comfort is not given only for our relief; it is given to be passed on. Your healing becomes someone else's medicine.

This reframes a leader's own wounds and hard seasons. The failure you survived, the grief you walked through, the doubt you came out of — these are not just private history. Comforted by God in them, you now hold a comfort uniquely fitted to others walking the same road. Leaders are often most useful to people not at the points of their strength but at the points of their healed weakness. Nothing you have suffered, if God has met you in it, is wasted. It is being stored up as comfort for someone else who will one day need exactly what you received.
voiceQuote: When once you have turned again, establish your brothers.
scriptureText: who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
weight:
The failure you survived, the grief you walked through — comforted by God, these become medicine uniquely fitted to others on the same road. Nothing you have suffered is wasted.

What comfort have you received in your own affliction that you could now pass on to someone walking the same road?

notes.primary: 2 Corinthians 1:3–4 (comfort others with the comfort you received); Luke 22:32 (turn again and strengthen your brothers).

leadership.principle: A leader's own comforted suffering becomes the resource for shepherding others through theirs. Healed weakness, not just strength, is where leaders are often most useful.
leadership.innerLife: Paul saw his afflictions as comfort stored up for others. A leader formed here lets God redeem his hard seasons into medicine for people on the same road. The inner work is believing nothing suffered, if God met him in it, is wasted.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Use the comfort you received in your own trials to comfort others in theirs. Lead from healed weakness, not just strength. Let your survived failures and griefs become a resource for the people walking where you have walked.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders hide their past wounds and lead only from strength, wasting their most useful resource. The blind spot is treating suffering as private history rather than comfort meant to be passed on.
leadership.difficultConversations: With someone in an affliction you have known, the most powerful comfort is your own, received from God. Sharing a healed wound can reach where untested strength cannot.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Recall one affliction in which God comforted you. This week, find someone on that same road and offer them the comfort you received.
teamQuestions: What comfort have we received that we could pass on?
Are we leading only from strength, hiding healed weakness?
Who is walking a road we have already survived?
Where might our past suffering be exactly what someone needs?

title: Carry them as a nurse
era: On the burden of carrying people
moment:
Crushed by the relentless complaints of a whole nation, Moses cries out to God in raw exasperation: did I conceive this people? Did I give them birth, that you tell me to carry them in my arms as a nurse carries a nursing infant? He is overwhelmed by the sheer weight of carrying people who never stop needing. It is one of the most honest moments in all of Scripture about the burden of leadership.

But buried in his complaint is the truth about the job. Leaders are, in fact, called to carry people — to bear them like a nurse bears an infant, with all the constant, exhausting, thankless tending that implies. Moses found it too heavy to carry alone, and God's answer was not to lower the level of care but to share the load among seventy others. The weight of carrying people is real, and a leader who feels crushed by it is not necessarily failing. But the load is meant to be shared, not denied. You are called to carry them — and you were never meant to carry them alone.
voiceQuote: Can a woman forget her nursing child? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you.
voiceAttribution: The LORD, of his unforgetting care — Isaiah 49:15 (WEB)
scriptureText: Have I conceived all this people? Have I brought them out, that you should tell me, Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing infant?
weight:
Carrying people — bearing them like a nurse bears an infant, with constant, exhausting, thankless tending — is genuinely heavy, and even Moses found it too heavy to carry alone.

Are you carrying your people as you are called to — and have you let others share a load that was never meant to be carried alone?

notes.primary: Numbers 11:11–17 (Moses, overwhelmed, told to carry the people; God shares the load among seventy); Isaiah 49:15 (God’s nursing, unforgetting care).

leadership.principle: Shepherding means carrying people, sometimes a crushing load. The honest leader admits the weight, keeps bearing it — and shares it, because it was never meant to be carried alone.
leadership.innerLife: Moses was honest about being crushed by the weight of the people. A leader formed here neither denies the burden nor tries to carry it solo. The inner work is bearing real weight while refusing to bear it alone.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Accept that carrying people is part of the calling, and feel free to admit when it is heavy. Then share the load, as God had Moses share it among seventy. Keep the level of care high while distributing the weight.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders either deny the weight of carrying people or insist on carrying it all alone until they collapse. The blind spot is treating an unshared, crushing load as a sign of faithfulness rather than a setup for failure.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a leader is crushed under the weight of people, the wise move is Moses’ — name it honestly and share the load, not lower the care. Admitting the burden is not weakness.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Name the heaviest part of carrying your people right now. This week, share that specific load with someone, instead of bearing it alone.
teamQuestions: Are we honest about how heavy carrying people can be?
Where are we trying to carry a load alone?
Whom could we share the weight with, as Moses shared it?
Are we keeping care high while distributing the burden?

title: Night and day, with tears
moment:
Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders is soaked in emotion. For three years, he reminds them, I never stopped warning each one of you, night and day, with tears. His leadership there was not detached oversight; it was tearful, persistent, deeply personal admonition — caring enough to warn, and warning long enough to weep.

We tend to separate love and admonition, as if warning people were the opposite of loving them. Paul fused the two. He admonished because he loved, and the tears proved the warnings were not contempt but care. Notice also the persistence: night and day, for three years — not a single dramatic confrontation, but a long faithfulness. Real shepherding includes the patient, repeated, often tearful work of warning people away from what will harm them. A leader who never warns does not love enough; a leader who warns without any tears has forgotten how.
voiceQuote: Many walk, of whom I tell you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ.
scriptureText: Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn't cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.
weight:
We separate love and admonition, as if warning people were the opposite of loving them. Paul fused them — he warned because he loved, and the tears proved it was care, not contempt.

Do you care enough to warn the people you lead — and do your warnings carry tears, or only edge?

notes.primary: Acts 20:31 (Paul admonished each one night and day with tears); Philippians 3:18 (warning even with weeping).

leadership.principle: Love and admonition belong together. A leader warns because he loves, and the tears prove the warning is care, not contempt — repeated patiently, not just once.
leadership.innerLife: Paul wept as he warned, fusing love and correction. A leader formed here cares enough to admonish and loves enough to do it with tears. The inner work is warning that flows from affection, not irritation.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Warn people away from what will harm them, patiently and repeatedly, out of love. Let your admonition carry warmth and even tears, not just edge. Treat persistent, caring warning as part of shepherding, not a breach of it.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders either avoid warning to seem kind or warn coldly and call it honesty. The blind spot is separating love from admonition, when the two were meant to be one.
leadership.difficultConversations: This is the difficult conversation done right — warning that is persistent and tear-stained, not a single cold confrontation. The tears tell the person the warning is for their good.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify one person you need to warn about something harmful. This week, do it — warmly, out of evident care, not just with edge.
teamQuestions: Do we care enough to warn, or do we avoid it to seem kind?
Do our warnings carry tears, or only edge?
Are we warning persistently, or just once and dropping it?
Where has love been divorced from admonition among us?

title: That they might be with him
moment:
When Jesus chose the Twelve, Mark records his purpose in a striking order: he appointed twelve that they might be with him, and to send them out to preach. Before the sending came the being-with. The primary qualification was not skill but proximity — they would be formed by sustained presence with him before they were ever deployed.

Most leadership development is impatient. We recruit people for what they can do and rush them into doing it. Jesus invested years in simply being with a few — eating, walking, talking, letting them watch him up close in success and strain alike. Deep formation happens through presence over time, not through programs. And he poured this into twelve, not a crowd. A leader who tries to develop everyone shallowly develops no one deeply. Jesus shows the opposite: invest deeply in a few, with being-together as the curriculum, and send them out genuinely formed.
voiceQuote: You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit.
scriptureText: He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.
weight:
We recruit people for what they can do and rush them into doing it. Jesus invested years in simply being with a few — being-with came before sending-out.

Are you investing deeply in a few through sustained presence, or developing everyone too shallowly to form anyone?

notes.primary: Mark 3:14 (appointed to be with him, then sent out); John 15:16 (I chose and appointed you to bear fruit).

leadership.principle: Deep formation happens through presence over time, not programs. Invest deeply in a few, with being-together as the curriculum, before sending them out.
leadership.innerLife: Jesus formed the Twelve by having them with him before deploying them. A leader formed here values sustained presence over quick recruitment, and depth in a few over breadth in many. The inner work is the patience to form people by proximity.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Spend real time with the few you are forming — let them watch you up close before you deploy them. Resist rushing people into doing before they have been with you. Choose depth in a few over shallow development of everyone.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders recruit for capability and skip the formative presence, then wonder why people are not deeply formed. The blind spot is mistaking deployment for development.
leadership.difficultConversations: When someone is sent out under-formed, the question is whether they were ever truly with the leader first. Presence, not just instruction, is what forms people.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Pick one person you are developing. This week, simply spend unhurried time with them, letting them see how you work, before assigning more.
teamQuestions: Are we forming people through presence, or only deploying them?
Whom are we investing in deeply enough to truly form?
Are we developing everyone shallowly instead of a few deeply?
Does being-with precede sending-out in how we lead?

title: Invite the ones who can't repay
moment:
At a dinner, Jesus tells the host to rethink his guest list. When you give a banquet, don't invite your friends, your family, or your rich neighbors — who will only invite you back. Invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. The kingdom guest list runs exactly opposite to the networking instinct.

Leaders naturally gather the useful and the impressive — the people who can advance the cause, repay the favor, reflect well on them. Jesus commends the opposite: making room for those who bring no advantage, who cannot repay, who are usually overlooked. It is a searching test of motive. The people you welcome into the work reveal whether you are building a kingdom or a network. Welcoming the overlooked and the least — those who can do nothing for you — is the mark of leadership that has stopped quietly keeping score.
voiceQuote: Didn't God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom?
voiceAttribution: James, on God's choice of the poor — James 2:5 (WEB)
scriptureText: But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind.
weight:
Leaders naturally gather the useful and impressive — those who can repay, advance the cause, reflect well on them. Jesus commends welcoming exactly those who can do none of that.

Whom are you welcoming into the work — the useful, or also the overlooked who can do nothing for you?

notes.primary: Luke 14:12–14 (invite those who cannot repay you); James 2:5 (God chose the poor to be rich in faith).

leadership.principle: Whom you welcome into the work reveals whether you are building a kingdom or a network. The mark of kingdom leadership is making room for those who can do nothing for you.
leadership.innerLife: Jesus reversed the networking instinct toward those who cannot repay. A leader formed here examines whether he gathers only the useful or also the overlooked. The inner work is welcoming people for their worth, not their usefulness.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Deliberately include the overlooked and the least, not just the impressive and useful. Build a team and a table that has room for those who bring no advantage. Let your guest list, not just your words, show what you are really building.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders gather the useful and call it strategy, quietly excluding those who cannot repay. The blind spot is mistaking a network for a kingdom because the score is always being kept.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a culture only values the useful, the corrective is to make visible room for the overlooked. Whom a leader welcomes teaches the team who counts.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Notice whom you keep including for their usefulness. This week, welcome someone overlooked who can do nothing for you, into the work or the room.
teamQuestions: Whom do we welcome — the useful, or also the overlooked?
Are we building a kingdom or a network?
Who can do nothing for us that we have left out?
Where are we quietly keeping score about who counts?

title: Strengthen the weak hands
moment:
Isaiah pictures a highway through the desert for God's redeemed people, and turns to those too exhausted to walk it with a command: strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to the anxious of heart, be strong, do not fear. The ones whose hands have dropped and whose knees have buckled are not to be left behind; others are to come alongside and put strength back into them.

It is a job description for leaders surrounded by tired people. Some on your team have weak hands — discouraged, drained, ready to quit. The instruction is not to shame them for their weakness but to strengthen it: to speak courage into the anxious, to firm up the buckling knees with help and hope. A leader is meant to be a source of strength to the depleted, not merely a demander of output from them. Wherever you find weak hands, your assignment is to put strength back into them.
voiceQuote: Your words have supported him who was falling, and you have made the feeble knees firm.
voiceAttribution: Eliphaz, of Job's past kindness — Job 4:4 (WEB)
scriptureText: Strengthen the weak hands, and make the feeble knees firm.
weight:
Some on your team have weak hands — discouraged, drained, ready to quit. The instruction is not to shame the weakness but to put strength back into it, with courage and help.

Where you find weak hands and buckling knees around you, are you strengthening them or just demanding more?

notes.primary: Isaiah 35:3–4 (strengthen weak hands and feeble knees; say to the anxious, be strong); Job 4:4 (words that strengthened the falling).

leadership.principle: A leader is a source of strength to the depleted, not just a demander of output. Where you find weak hands and buckling knees, the job is to put strength back into them.
leadership.innerLife: Isaiah sends the strong to strengthen the failing rather than leave them behind. A leader formed here responds to weakness with help and courage, not shame. The inner work is becoming a source of strength to the tired.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Come alongside the discouraged and drained and put strength back into them — speak courage, firm up the buckling, offer real help. Refuse to shame weakness or simply demand more from it. Be a supply of strength, not only a draw on it.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders meet weak hands with more demands and read exhaustion as a performance problem. The blind spot is failing to strengthen the depleted, so the weak are left behind.
leadership.difficultConversations: With someone whose hands have dropped, the needed word is courage and help, not rebuke. Strengthening the weak often does more than pressing them harder.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Find one person with weak hands on your team. This week, do something concrete to put strength back into them.
teamQuestions: Who around us has weak hands and buckling knees?
Are we strengthening the depleted or just demanding more?
Do we respond to weakness with help or with shame?
Are we a source of strength, or only a draw on it?

title: Fan into flame
moment:
Paul urges Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God that is in him. The image assumes the fire is already there — a real gift, given by God, but burning low and in danger of dying down to embers. Paul's task is not to give Timothy a gift but to stir up the one he already has, to blow on the coals until they blaze again.

Much of developing people is exactly this: not installing ability they lack, but fanning gifts that are present yet dormant. People carry undeveloped, discouraged, half-buried gifts, and a leader's words can either let them smolder out or breathe them into flame. The leader who only assigns tasks misses this entirely. The leader who develops people goes looking for the buried gift and fans it — naming it, calling it out, blowing steadily on coals the person may not even know are still warm.
voiceQuote: Don't quench the Spirit.
voiceAttribution: Paul, on the Spirit's fire — 1 Thessalonians 5:19 (WEB)
scriptureText: For this cause, I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.
weight:
People carry undeveloped, discouraged, half-buried gifts, and a leader's words either let them smolder out or breathe them into flame.

Whose buried or low-burning gift could you fan into flame — and whose are you letting smolder out?

notes.primary: 2 Timothy 1:6 (stir up the gift that is in you); 1 Thessalonians 5:19 (do not quench the Spirit).

leadership.principle: Developing people is often not installing ability but fanning dormant gifts. A leader’s words breathe a buried gift into flame, or let it smolder out.
leadership.innerLife: Paul saw a real gift in Timothy that needed stirring, not supplying. A leader formed here looks for the latent gift in people and blows on the coals. The inner work is believing the fire is already there to be fanned.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Go looking for the buried or discouraged gifts in your people and call them out. Name what you see, give it room, and keep fanning until it blazes. Develop people by stirring what is in them, not just assigning tasks.
leadership.blindSpot: Task-focused leaders never notice the dormant gifts around them and let them die to embers. The blind spot is assuming development means adding skills rather than fanning what is already present.
leadership.difficultConversations: Sometimes the most developmental word is naming a gift someone has buried under discouragement. Fanning it can do more than any assignment.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Spot one low-burning gift in someone you lead. This week, name it to them and give it one concrete chance to flame up.
teamQuestions: Whose gift could we fan into flame?
Whose are we letting smolder out?
Are we developing people or only assigning tasks?
What latent gifts around us have we never named?

title: They will know by your love
moment:
On his last night, Jesus gives his disciples a new commandment and stakes the whole credibility of their witness on it: love one another, as I have loved you. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples — if you have love for one another. Not by their doctrine, their success, or their strategy, but by their love for each other, the watching world would know whose they were.

It is the capstone of shepherding. The way leaders and their people treat one another is itself the message. A community marked by genuine love preaches what no program can; a community marked by rivalry, coldness, or contempt discredits whatever it claims. For a leader this means the relationships you cultivate are not separate from the mission — they are the mission's proof. People will know what you are really about far less by what you say than by how those in your care actually love one another.
voiceQuote: If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.
voiceAttribution: John, on love made complete — 1 John 4:12 (WEB)
scriptureText: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.
weight:
People will know what you are really about less by what you say than by how those in your care treat one another. Love is the proof — or its absence the disproof — of everything you claim.

Would the love among your people convince a watching world, or quietly discredit everything you stand for?

notes.primary: John 13:34–35 (love one another; by this all will know); 1 John 4:12 (love one another and God’s love is perfected in us).

leadership.principle: The way a community loves one another is itself the message. Relationships are not separate from the mission; they are its proof to a watching world.
leadership.innerLife: Jesus tied his disciples’ credibility to their love for each other. A leader formed here treats the quality of relationships as central to the mission, not incidental. The inner work is building love, not just output, among his people.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Cultivate genuine love among your people as part of the mission, not a distraction from it. Confront rivalry, coldness, and contempt as threats to the witness. Let how your community treats one another be its most persuasive message.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders pursue results and treat relationships as secondary, not seeing that the love among their people is the actual proof. The blind spot is a community whose internal coldness discredits its claims.
leadership.difficultConversations: When rivalry or contempt festers, the stakes are the whole witness. Addressing how people treat one another is mission-critical, not interpersonal housekeeping.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Assess the love among your people honestly. This week, take one step to heal a cold or rivalrous relationship on your team.
teamQuestions: Would the love among us convince a watching world?
Where do rivalry or coldness discredit what we claim?
Do we treat relationships as the mission’s proof, or a distraction?
How do those in our care actually treat one another?

title: Too heavy to carry alone
era: On refusing to do it all
moment:
Jethro watches his son-in-law judge the people from morning to evening, a line stretching out before Moses all day long, and gives him a blunt assessment: what you are doing is not good. You will surely wear yourself out, and these people with you, for the task is too heavy; you are not able to do it alone. It is the first leadership consultation in Scripture, and the diagnosis is a do-it-all leader heading for collapse.

Jethro names two casualties of the leader who refuses to share the load: the leader, who burns out, and the people, who are underserved while everything bottlenecks through one exhausted person. Carrying alone what others could share is not heroism; it is a slow disaster for everyone involved. The wise leader hears Jethro out: some work is genuinely too heavy to do alone, and refusing help does not prove strength — it guarantees breakdown, sooner or later, for the leader and the led alike.
voiceQuote: I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.
scriptureText: You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
weight:
Carrying alone what others could share is not heroism; it is a slow disaster — the leader burns out, and the people are underserved while everything bottlenecks through one person.

What are you carrying alone that is wearing you out — and whom could you share it with before you break?

notes.primary: Exodus 18:13–18 (Jethro warns Moses he cannot do it alone); Numbers 11:14 (Moses: it is too heavy for me).

leadership.principle: Some work is too heavy to do alone. Refusing to share the load is not strength but a slow disaster — for the leader who burns out and the people left underserved.
leadership.innerLife: Jethro confronted Moses’ do-it-all pattern before it broke him. A leader formed here admits when a load is too heavy and refuses the false heroism of carrying it solo. The inner work is letting go of the need to be the one through whom everything passes.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Identify what is too heavy to carry alone and share it before you collapse. Watch for the bottleneck you have become. Treat distributing the load as wisdom, not weakness.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders equate carrying everything with strength and miss the breakdown coming for them and their people. The blind spot is mistaking the bottleneck for indispensability.
leadership.difficultConversations: Sometimes the needed word is Jethro's: what you are doing is not good. Telling an overloaded leader to share the load is a kindness, not a criticism.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Name the heaviest thing you are carrying alone. This week, hand a real piece of it to someone else before it wears you out.
teamQuestions: What are we carrying alone that is wearing us out?
Where have we become the bottleneck?
Whom could we share the load with before we break?
Are we mistaking doing it all for strength?

title: Appoint capable people
moment:
Jethro does not just diagnose; he prescribes a structure. Choose able men from all the people — men who fear God, are trustworthy, and hate dishonest gain — and appoint them as leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Build layers of capable, character-tested leaders, and let them handle all but the hardest cases, which alone come to Moses.

Notice Jethro's criteria. The first qualifications are not talent or charisma but character: God-fearing, trustworthy, incorruptible. Then capability — able men. A leader multiplying himself must choose for character first, because he is distributing not just work but authority, and authority in the hands of the gifted-but-untrustworthy is dangerous. Notice too the tiered structure — leaders over tens as well as thousands — so no one carries an impossible span and everyone has someone close enough to help. Good delegation is not merely offloading work; it is building the right people into the right structure.
voiceQuote: Take wise men of understanding, and well known according to your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.
scriptureText: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.
weight:
A leader multiplying himself distributes not just work but authority — and authority in untrustworthy hands is dangerous. So Jethro's first criteria were character: God-fearing, trustworthy, incorruptible.

Are you choosing people for the right things — character first, then capability — when you hand them authority?

notes.primary: Exodus 18:21–23 (appoint able, God-fearing, trustworthy men over tiered groups); Deuteronomy 1:13 (choose wise, understanding men as heads).

leadership.principle: Good delegation chooses for character first, then capability, and builds the right people into the right structure. You are distributing authority, not just work.
leadership.innerLife: Jethro prized God-fearing trustworthiness above talent. A leader formed here weighs character before charisma when handing out authority. The inner work is valuing trustworthiness in those he empowers, not just ability.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Select people for character — integrity, the fear of God, incorruptibility — and then for capability. Build manageable spans so no one is overloaded and everyone has help nearby. Design structure, not just hand off tasks.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders delegate to the talented without testing character and hand authority to the untrustworthy. The blind spot is treating delegation as offloading work rather than distributing power.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a gifted but untrustworthy person seeks authority, the hard call is to choose character over talent. Authority misplaced does more damage than work left undone.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Review whom you have given authority. This week, weigh one delegation by character first, and adjust the structure so spans are manageable.
teamQuestions: Are we choosing for character first, then capability?
Where have we handed authority to the merely talented?
Are our spans manageable, with help close by?
Are we designing structure, or just offloading tasks?

title: Distribute the burden
moment:
Moses, crushed and ready to die under the weight of the people, hears God's remedy: gather seventy of the elders, and I will take of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you do not bear it alone. God's solution to one overwhelmed leader is not a stronger Moses but a shared Spirit and a distributed load.

There is something profound here. God was willing to take the very Spirit resting on Moses and spread it across seventy others. The anointing was not hoarded in one man; it was distributed so the burden could be too. Leaders who believe everything depends on their unique gifting resist this — surely no one else can carry what I carry. God says otherwise. He multiplies the gift in order to multiply the carriers. The load you think only you can bear is, in fact, meant to be distributed — and there is enough Spirit to equip those who will share it.
voiceQuote: Aaron and Hur held up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side.
voiceAttribution: Of Aaron and Hur, holding up Moses — Exodus 17:12 (WEB)
scriptureText: I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
weight:
Leaders who believe everything depends on their unique gifting resist sharing the load — surely no one else can carry what I carry. God multiplied the gift to multiply the carriers.

What load are you convinced only you can bear — and is God inviting you to distribute it among others?

notes.primary: Numbers 11:16–17 (God shares the Spirit on Moses among seventy to bear the burden); Exodus 17:12 (Aaron and Hur hold up Moses’ hands).

leadership.principle: God multiplies the gift to multiply the carriers. The load you think only you can bear is meant to be distributed, and there is enough to equip those who share it.
leadership.innerLife: God spread the Spirit on Moses across seventy rather than strengthening one man. A leader formed here releases the belief that everything depends on his unique gifting. The inner work is trusting others to genuinely carry the load with him.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Distribute the burden by empowering others to truly share it, not just assist. Trust that the gift can be multiplied, and equip people to carry real weight. Refuse to hoard either the load or the anointing.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders believe no one else can carry what they carry and so carry it until they break. The blind spot is hoarding the burden under the guise of unique gifting.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a leader insists only he can do it, the freeing truth is that God distributes gifts to distribute loads. Sharing the burden is not lowering the standard.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Name a burden you believe only you can carry. This week, genuinely share it with someone, trusting them to carry real weight.
teamQuestions: What load are we convinced only we can bear?
Are we distributing the burden, or just assigning helpers?
Do we trust others to carry real weight?
Where are we hoarding the load under "unique gifting"?

title: Choose proven people
moment:
When the early church hit its first administrative crisis — Greek-speaking widows being overlooked in the daily distribution — the apostles did not simply solve it themselves. They told the community: choose seven men from among you of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, and we will appoint them over this task. They delegated a real problem to proven, qualified people and freed themselves for prayer and the word.

The criteria are worth noting. Good repute, full of the Spirit, full of wisdom — even for what looked like a practical, logistical job of waiting on tables. The church did not hand the work to whoever happened to be available, but to whoever was proven. Good delegation matches real responsibility with genuinely qualified people. Offload to the unready and you simply create new crises; entrust to the proven and you multiply the whole community's capacity. The quality of those you choose decides whether delegation relieves your problems or multiplies them.
voiceQuote: Let them also first be tested; then let them serve, if they are blameless.
voiceAttribution: Paul, on testing before appointing — 1 Timothy 3:10 (WEB)
scriptureText: Therefore select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
weight:
Offload to the unready and you create new crises; entrust to the proven and you multiply capacity. Even for waiting tables, the church chose people full of the Spirit and wisdom.

Are you matching real responsibility with genuinely proven people, or handing it to whoever is simply available?

notes.primary: Acts 6:1–4 (choose seven proven, Spirit-filled men for the task); 1 Timothy 3:10 (test people before they serve).

leadership.principle: Good delegation matches real responsibility with proven people. Offload to the unready and you create new crises; entrust to the qualified and you multiply capacity.
leadership.innerLife: The apostles delegated a real problem to tested, Spirit-filled people. A leader formed here resists handing responsibility to whoever is merely available. The inner work is the discipline to entrust weight only to the proven.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Delegate real responsibility to people of proven character and wisdom, even for practical jobs. Test readiness before you hand over weight. Free yourself for your essential work by entrusting the rest to the qualified.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders delegate to whoever is available and then firefight the crises that follow. The blind spot is treating delegation as offloading rather than matching weight to proven capacity.
leadership.difficultConversations: When an eager but unready person wants responsibility, the wise word is first be tested. Matching weight to readiness prevents the crises premature delegation creates.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Take one thing you need to delegate. This week, entrust it to a genuinely proven person rather than whoever is simply free.
teamQuestions: Are we matching responsibility to proven people?
Where have we handed weight to whoever was available?
Do we test readiness before delegating?
Is our delegation relieving problems or multiplying them?

title: Two are better than one
moment:
The Preacher, who has spent chapters exposing the vanity of so much human effort, pauses on one solid good: two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. He lists the payoffs — if one falls, the other lifts him; if two lie down together, they keep warm; a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. Partnership multiplies effectiveness and cushions failure.

Solo leadership feels efficient and is secretly fragile. The lone leader has no one to lift him when he falls, no one to keep him warm in the cold seasons, no one to add strength when his own runs out. Two are simply better — not just more productive, but more resilient. The wise leader does not prize his independence as a virtue; he builds partnership, because the work goes further and survives more when it is not carried by one set of hands alone.
voiceQuote: Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?
scriptureText: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
weight:
Solo leadership feels efficient and is secretly fragile — no one to lift you when you fall, no one to add strength when yours runs out.

Where are you leading alone that you should be leading in partnership — and what fragility is your independence hiding?

notes.primary: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 (two are better than one); Amos 3:3 (two walking together in agreement).

leadership.principle: Partnership multiplies effectiveness and cushions failure. Solo leadership feels efficient but is secretly fragile; two are better than one, not just more productive but more resilient.
leadership.innerLife: The Preacher prized partnership over solitary toil. A leader formed here stops treating independence as a virtue and builds genuine partnership. The inner work is admitting he is stronger, and safer, with others than alone.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Build partnership into how you lead, so someone can lift you when you fall and add strength when yours runs out. Resist the fragile efficiency of going solo. Value resilience, not just productivity, in how the work is carried.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders prize self-sufficiency and miss how fragile solo leadership is. The blind spot is mistaking independence for strength while quietly removing every safeguard a partner would provide.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a leader insists on going it alone, the caring challenge is that two are better than one. It names the hidden fragility of his independence.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify one area you lead entirely alone. This week, bring in a genuine partner to share it, not just a helper.
teamQuestions: Where are we leading alone that we should lead in partnership?
What fragility is our independence hiding?
Who would lift us if we fell right now?
Are we valuing resilience, or only efficiency?

title: A threefold cord
moment:
The Preacher caps his case for partnership with an image from rope-making: though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves, and a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. A single thread snaps easily; braid three together and the cord holds weight that would break any one of them alone. The strength is not in the individual strand but in the binding.

Teams work the same way. A leader standing alone can be overpowered — by opposition, by discouragement, by his own blind spots. Bound together with others, he becomes part of something far harder to break. The lesson is not merely to add people, but to bind them — to weave genuine, committed relationships rather than just assemble individuals. A bag of loose threads is still weak; a braided cord is strong. The leader's real task is to do the braiding.
voiceQuote: The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
scriptureText: If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
weight:
A bag of loose threads is still weak; only a braided cord is strong. Adding people is not enough — they have to be bound together into something hard to break.

Are you braiding your people into a strong cord, or just collecting loose threads?

notes.primary: Ecclesiastes 4:12 (a threefold cord is not quickly broken); 1 Samuel 18:1 (Jonathan’s soul knit to David’s).

leadership.principle: Strength is in the binding, not the individual strand. A leader’s task is not just to add people but to braid them into committed relationships hard to break.
leadership.innerLife: The Preacher locates strength in the braided cord, not the lone thread. A leader formed here invests in binding people together, not merely gathering them. The inner work is valuing committed bonds over a collection of individuals.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Braid your people together through genuine, committed relationships, not just shared tasks. Build bonds that can withstand opposition and discouragement. Do the work of weaving, so the team is a cord, not a bundle of loose threads.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders assemble talented individuals and assume that makes a team. The blind spot is mistaking a bag of loose threads for a braided cord.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a group is strong individually but weak together, the issue is the binding. Naming the lack of real bonds is the first step to braiding them.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Look at your team as threads. This week, take one concrete step to bind two or more of them into a stronger, committed relationship.
teamQuestions: Are we braided into a cord, or just collected as threads?
How strong are the bonds between our people?
Where would we snap because we are not bound together?
What braiding work is ours to do?

title: Many members, one body
figure: Paul on the body and its parts
moment:
Paul confronts a divided church with the image of a body. The foot cannot say, because I am not a hand, I do not belong. The eye cannot tell the hand, I have no need of you. God arranged the members, every one of them, in the body just as he willed — and the parts that seem weaker are, in fact, indispensable. A body is not a collection of identical parts but a diversity of necessary ones.

Leaders are tempted toward two errors the body image corrects. The first is undervaluing people who are different — wishing everyone were a hand and quietly dismissing the feet. The second is letting the strong despise the weak as unnecessary. Paul insists every member is needed, especially the ones that seem least impressive. A leader's job is to help each person find and value their own part, and to build a body where difference is the strength, not a problem to be standardized away.
voiceQuote: From whom all the body... according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase.
voiceAttribution: Paul, on the body that builds itself up — Ephesians 4:16 (WEB)
scriptureText: But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.
weight:
Leaders are tempted to wish everyone were a hand and dismiss the feet — to standardize away difference. Paul says the parts that seem weaker are indispensable.

Are you building a body where difference is the strength, or quietly wishing everyone were the same?

notes.primary: 1 Corinthians 12:14–21 (the body has many necessary members); Ephesians 4:16 (each part working makes the body grow).

leadership.principle: A team is a body of diverse, necessary parts, not a collection of identical ones. Difference is the strength, and the members that seem weaker are indispensable.
leadership.innerLife: Paul saw the necessity of every member, especially the unimpressive. A leader formed here values difference instead of wishing everyone were the same. The inner work is honoring the parts that do not look strong.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Help each person find and value their part, and build a team where difference is an asset. Resist standardizing people into copies of the strong. Honor the indispensable, less impressive members rather than sidelining them.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders favor people like themselves and undervalue different gifts, weakening the body. The blind spot is treating difference as a problem to fix rather than the strength it is.
leadership.difficultConversations: When someone feels useless or is being dismissed as unnecessary, the truth is that the body needs them. It restores the value of a member the team had written off.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify a team member whose different gift you undervalue. This week, name and make room for the part only they can play.
teamQuestions: Do we treat difference as strength or as a problem?
Whom are we dismissing as unnecessary?
Are we wishing everyone were the same kind of part?
Does each person know and value their role in the body?

title: Two by two
moment:
When Jesus first sends out the Twelve, he does something easy to overlook: he sends them two by two. He could have doubled the reach by sending them singly, but he paired them instead. The mission was important enough to sacrifice coverage for companionship — because people sent alone are vulnerable in ways people sent together are not.

There is wisdom here about how to deploy people. Alone, a person has no one to encourage them when it goes badly, no one to check their judgment, no one to share the load or witness the work. Jesus builds companionship into the very structure of the mission. The instinct to maximize coverage by spreading people thin and solo often backfires; a supportive pair accomplishes more, and survives more, than two isolated individuals. When you send people out, send them out together.
voiceQuote: The Lord appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him.
voiceAttribution: Of the seventy Jesus sent — Luke 10:1 (WEB)
scriptureText: He called to himself the twelve, and began to send them out two by two; and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
weight:
We maximize coverage by spreading people thin and solo. Jesus sacrificed reach for partnership, pairing his workers — because people sent alone are vulnerable in ways the paired are not.

Are you sending your people out alone to cover more ground, or pairing them so they can endure and check each other?

notes.primary: Mark 6:7 (sent out two by two with authority); Luke 10:1 (the seventy sent two by two).

leadership.principle: People sent alone are vulnerable in ways the paired are not. It is often worth sacrificing reach for companionship when you deploy people.
leadership.innerLife: Jesus valued companionship in mission enough to halve his coverage. A leader formed here resists spreading people thin and solo for the sake of reach. The inner work is prioritizing people’s endurance over maximum coverage.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Send people out in pairs or supported teams, not isolated and alone. Build encouragement, accountability, and shared load into the structure of assignments. Accept less reach when partnership makes the work more durable.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders maximize coverage by isolating people and call it efficiency. The blind spot is not seeing how vulnerable solo deployment leaves them.
leadership.difficultConversations: When someone is struggling alone in the field, the question is whether they were ever paired. Adding a partner can rescue what isolation was breaking.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Find one person you have sent out alone. This week, pair them with someone for support, accountability, and shared load.
teamQuestions: Are we sending people out alone to cover more ground?
Who is isolated in their assignment right now?
Where would pairing make the work more durable?
Are we prioritizing reach over our people’s endurance?

title: Would that all were prophets
moment:
When two men, Eldad and Medad, began prophesying in the camp outside the official gathering, Joshua was alarmed and urged Moses to stop them. Moses' reply is one of the most generous lines any leader ever spoke: are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his Spirit on them all! Where Joshua saw a threat to Moses' unique standing, Moses saw a hope to be celebrated.

Insecure leaders guard their gift jealously, threatened when others rise, eager to keep the anointing scarce and centered on themselves. Moses wanted the opposite — for the gift to spread to everyone, for leaders to multiply beyond counting, even at the cost of his own uniqueness. A leader's security is tested by how he responds when others share or even exceed his gift. The great ones wish it on everybody. They are not protecting their own indispensability; they are multiplying leaders.
voiceQuote: Don't forbid him, for there is no one who will do a mighty work in my name, and be able quickly to speak evil of me.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, on the outsider doing good — Mark 9:39 (WEB)
scriptureText: Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!
weight:
Insecure leaders guard their gift jealously, threatened when others rise. Moses wished his anointing on everyone, even at the cost of his own uniqueness.

When someone else rises, shares, or exceeds your gift, are you threatened — or do you wish it on everybody?

notes.primary: Numbers 11:26–29 (Moses wishes all the LORD’s people were prophets); Mark 9:39 (do not forbid the outsider doing good).

leadership.principle: A leader's security is tested by how he responds when others share or exceed his gift. The great ones multiply leaders and wish the gift on everyone.
leadership.innerLife: Moses celebrated others’ anointing where Joshua felt threatened. A leader formed here roots his security deep enough to rejoice when others rise. The inner work is wanting the gift multiplied more than wanting to be unique.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Actively multiply leaders and celebrate when others share or exceed your gift. Refuse to keep the anointing scarce and centered on yourself. Build others’ indispensability, not your own.
leadership.blindSpot: Insecure leaders guard their gift and subtly suppress rising others. The blind spot is mistaking the protection of their own uniqueness for stewardship.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a team member begins to outshine the leader, the gracious response is Moses’ — would that all were so gifted. It exposes and heals territorial insecurity.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Notice where someone rising makes you uneasy. This week, deliberately celebrate and multiply their gift instead of guarding your own.
teamQuestions: When others rise, are we threatened or glad?
Are we multiplying leaders or guarding our uniqueness?
Where do we keep the gift scarce and centered on us?
Do we build others’ indispensability or only our own?

title: Know the God of your father
moment:
Near the end of his life, David hands the great work of the temple to his son Solomon, and his charge is striking in its order. Before any blueprint or budget, David says: know the God of your father, and serve him with a whole heart and a willing mind. Then, and only then: be strong, and do the work. The succession begins not with transferring tasks but with transferring the foundation — a relationship with God.

Leaders preparing successors often pass on systems, skills, and strategies, but neglect the deepest thing. David knew the temple would stand or fall not on Solomon's competence but on his heart toward God. Preparing the next generation means handing down more than know-how; it means forming the character and faith on which everything else rests. The succession David cared about most was not of a throne or a project, but of a devotion. Build that into your successor first, and the work has a foundation; neglect it, and the most capable heir is building on sand.
voiceQuote: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.
scriptureText: You, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind.
weight:
Leaders preparing successors pass on systems, skills, and strategies, but neglect the deepest thing — the heart on which everything else rests. David charged Solomon to know God first, then build.

Are you preparing your successor's character and faith, or only handing down know-how?

notes.primary: 1 Chronicles 28:9–10 (David charges Solomon to know God, then build); Proverbs 22:6 (train up a child in the way).

leadership.principle: Succession transfers a foundation, not just tasks. Preparing the next generation means forming the character and faith on which everything else rests, before the know-how.
leadership.innerLife: David put knowing God before building the temple in his charge to Solomon. A leader formed here invests first in a successor’s heart, not only his skills. The inner work is caring more about the foundation than the output.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Form your successors’ character and faith before transferring systems and strategies. Make the deepest things — devotion, integrity, the heart toward God — the heart of your handoff. Build the foundation, then the work.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders pass on competence and neglect character, leaving capable heirs on a weak foundation. The blind spot is mistaking the transfer of know-how for genuine preparation.
leadership.difficultConversations: When grooming a successor, the deepest conversations are about character and devotion, not just skills. David’s order — know God first — should shape the handoff.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Take one person you are preparing. This week, invest in their character or faith, not just their competence.
teamQuestions: Are we forming successors’ character, or only their skills?
What foundation are we handing down?
Where are capable heirs building on sand?
Does our succession transfer devotion, not just know-how?

title: He goes before you
moment:
With his death near, Moses calls Joshua before all Israel and commissions him publicly. Be strong and courageous, he says, for you will bring this people into the land. And then he points past himself to the real source of confidence: it is the LORD who goes before you; he will be with you; he will never leave you nor forsake you. A good handoff does not anchor the successor to the departing leader, but to the God who outlasts them both.

The temptation in succession is to make the successor dependent on you — to leave them clinging to your guidance, your presence, your way of doing things. Moses does the opposite. He releases Joshua not into his own absence but into God's presence. The point of a good handoff is that the work no longer depends on the predecessor being there; it depends on God, who goes before the next leader exactly as he went before the last. Hand people off to God, not to your shadow.
voiceQuote: The works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, on those who follow — John 14:12 (WEB)
scriptureText: The LORD himself is who goes before you. He will be with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you. Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed.
weight:
The temptation in succession is to leave the successor dependent on you — clinging to your presence and your way. Moses released Joshua not into his own absence, but into God's presence.

When you hand off, are you anchoring people to yourself, or to the God who will go before them when you're gone?

notes.primary: Deuteronomy 31:7–8 (Moses commissions Joshua; the LORD goes before you); John 14:12 (followers will do greater works).

leadership.principle: A good handoff anchors the successor to God, not to the departing leader. The work should depend on God who goes before the next leader, not on the predecessor’s presence.
leadership.innerLife: Moses pointed Joshua past himself to the God who goes before. A leader formed here releases successors into God’s presence rather than his own shadow. The inner work is wanting people anchored to God, not dependent on him.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Hand people off to God and to their own footing, not to ongoing dependence on you. Build successors who can stand when you are gone. Point past yourself to the One who will go before them.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders leave successors dependent on their guidance and call it support. The blind spot is anchoring people to themselves so the work cannot outlast their presence.
leadership.difficultConversations: A clean handoff sometimes means telling a successor to stop leaning on you and lean on God. Releasing them fully is harder, and kinder, than keeping them dependent.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Identify someone overly dependent on you. This week, take one step to anchor them to God and their own footing instead of your shadow.
teamQuestions: Are we anchoring people to ourselves or to God?
Would the work survive our absence?
Whom have we left dependent on our presence?
Are we pointing successors past ourselves?

title: A double portion
moment:
As Elijah's departure nears, he turns to Elisha with a remarkable offer: ask what I shall do for you before I am taken from you. And Elisha asks for the boldest thing imaginable — a double portion of your spirit. He does not want merely to continue Elijah's ministry; he wants twice the power. Elijah does not rebuke the ambition. He calls it a hard thing, but says that if Elisha sees him taken up, it will be his. The mentor blesses the protégé's desire to exceed him.

This is the secret heart of great succession: equipping the next generation not merely to maintain what you built, but to surpass it. Small leaders want successors who will be slightly lesser copies, preserving their legacy without ever threatening it. Great leaders, like Elijah, want their successors to go further than they did — and they give themselves to making it possible. The measure of your leadership is not how high you rose, but how much higher you enabled those who came after you to climb.
voiceQuote: He must increase, but I must decrease.
voiceAttribution: John the Baptist, on stepping aside — John 3:30 (WEB)
scriptureText: Elijah said to Elisha, Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you. Elisha said, Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.
weight:
