The instinct in chaos is to do more, move faster, take control. God's command is the opposite: be still, and know that I am God. The leader who cannot be still is too busy trying to be God himself.

In the upheavals you face, can you be still enough to know that he is God?

notes.primary: Psalm 46:10 (be still and know that I am God); Exodus 14:14 (the LORD will fight for you; be still).

leadership.principle: In upheaval, the command is not more frantic activity but stillness — a deliberate ceasing in order to know that God is God and you are not.
leadership.innerLife: The psalm calls the leader to be still amid chaos. A leader formed here stops striving long enough to know God. The inner work is stillness that resists the urge to control everything.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: When things shake, be still before God rather than only doing more. Lead from the steadiness that knowing God provides. Let deliberate stillness, not frantic control, anchor you and your team.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders respond to chaos by doing more and taking control, never being still. The blind spot is being too busy trying to be God to actually know him.
leadership.difficultConversations: In a crisis, the steadying move can be stillness before God, not frantic action. Being still long enough to know him reorders everything that follows.
leadership.weeklyPractice: In the next upheaval you face, deliberately be still before God before acting, long enough to know that he is God.
teamQuestions: In upheaval, can we be still enough to know that he is God?
Do we respond to chaos by doing more and taking control?
Where are we too busy trying to be God to know him?
How does stillness before God steady our leadership?

title: His counsel stands forever
figure: The psalm on God’s settled purpose
era: On the plan that outlasts all
moment:
The psalmist ends a meditation on God's sovereignty with a settled certainty: the counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations. Nations rage, kings rise and fall, human plans come and go — but God's counsel stands, unshaken, across every generation. What he has purposed will be done; his plans outlast every other plan.

This is where a year of leadership principles finally rests. After all the calling and character, the wisdom and courage, the shepherding and the suffering, the failures and the prayers — the last word is that God's counsel stands forever. Your leadership, however faithful, is a brief chapter in a story whose author is God, and whose ending he has already secured. This is the deepest freedom a leader can know: you are not holding the world together, and you do not have to. Your task is simply to align your small, faithful part with the plans of his heart, which will surely come to pass.
voiceQuote: My counsel will stand, and I will do all that I please.
scriptureText: The counsel of the LORD stands fast forever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations.
weight:
After all the calling, character, courage, and prayer, the last word is this: God's counsel stands forever. You are not holding the world together, and you don't have to — your task is to align your brief, faithful part with his eternal plans.

Does your leadership rest in the settled certainty that God's counsel stands forever?

notes.primary: Psalm 33:11 (the counsel of the LORD stands forever); Isaiah 46:10 (my counsel will stand).

leadership.principle: God's counsel stands forever, outlasting every human plan. A leader's work is a brief, faithful chapter in a story whose author is God and whose ending is already secured.
leadership.innerLife: The psalm rests everything on God’s unshakable, eternal purpose. A leader formed here finds freedom in not having to hold the world together. The inner work is aligning his small part with the plans of God’s heart, which will surely come to pass.
leadership.leadingThroughIt: Lead from the settled certainty that God’s counsel stands forever. Hold your plans humbly within his eternal ones. Free yourself and your team from the burden of securing the outcome God has already secured.
leadership.blindSpot: Leaders act as if they are holding the world together and everything depends on their plans. The blind spot is forgetting that God’s counsel, not theirs, has the final and lasting word.
leadership.difficultConversations: When a leader or team is crushed by the weight of outcomes, the freeing truth is that God’s counsel stands forever. Their faithful part matters within a story he has already secured.
leadership.weeklyPractice: Name a burden you carry as if everything depended on your plans. This week, rest it in the certainty that God’s counsel stands forever, and align your part with his.
teamQuestions: Does our leadership rest in the certainty that God’s counsel stands forever?
Are we acting as if we hold the world together?
Do we hold our plans humbly within God’s eternal ones?
How does God’s secured ending free us to lead faithfully?
